artworks.title: Plate with Hypermnestra Watching Lynceus Take Her Father's Crown
artworks.description: This maiolica plate by Francesco Xanto Avelli (Walters Art Museum 48.1324) shows Hypermnestra — the one Danaid who spared her husband Lynceus — watching him seize her father Danaus' crown. Renaissance tin-glaze turns the Argive exception into a political allegory of mercy rewarded: the sister who refused the wedding-night massacre becomes queen-maker. It is among the rare works that name Hypermnestra apart from the mass of forty-nine killers.

artworks.title: Hypermnestra Writing
artworks.description: In this BnF manuscript miniature (Français 874), Hypermnestra sits writing — the Ovidian heroine of Heroides XIV, the Danaid who spared Lynceus and writes to him from imprisonment. Medieval book-art freezes her as a letter-writer rather than a murderess, the literary afterlife that made her the conscience of Danaus' house.

artworks.title: The Danaids Killing Their Husbands
artworks.description: This BnF miniature (Français 874) stages the wedding-night massacre Hypermnestra alone refused: Danaus' daughters slay the sons of Aegyptus in their beds. The image is the visual foil to her mercy — the crime that defines the Danaids' underworld punishment and makes her the single exception named by Ovid and Apollodorus.

popCulture.title: Heroides XIV (Hypermnestra to Lynceus)
popCulture.creator: Ovid
popCulture.description: Ovid's verse letter lets Hypermnestra speak — the Danaid who spared her husband and writes from chains, the defining Roman reception of her mercy.

popCulture.title: The Suppliants
popCulture.creator: Aeschylus
popCulture.description: Aeschylus' Danaid play brings Danaus' daughters to Argos as suppliants — the tragic cycle whose aftermath makes Hypermnestra the one bride who will not kill.
